questions.stem: Which reaction is an addition?

options.explanation: Two reactants become one product across the double bond - the addition signature.
Two products from two reactant fragments with substitution running the show.
One reactant yielding two products is elimination.
That is oxidation of an aldehyde.

questions.stem: Elimination reactions are usually recognised because

options.text: Oxygen is gained by the organic compound
options.explanation: Oxygen gain marks oxidation.

options.text: More products form than reactants, often an alkene plus a small molecule
options.explanation: The castoff small molecule plus the unsaturated organic product mark elimination.

options.text: Two reactants form exactly one product
options.explanation: That is addition, the opposite census.

options.text: An atom is swapped for another atom
options.explanation: That is substitution.

questions.stem: Ethene reacting with water forms ethanol by

options.explanation: Nothing is eliminated; bond count falls.
Hydrogen is gained, but the pattern is addition.
Water adds across C=C to give the saturated alcohol.
No atom is swapped; the whole water molecule adds.

questions.stem: Bromoethane with hydroxide can follow two different pathways: to ethanol (substitution) or to ethene plus water and bromide (elimination). The distinguishing feature of the elimination route is

options.explanation: Elimination breaks the C-Br bond, ejecting bromide.
The double bond is created here, not consumed.

options.text: Addition of hydroxide across a double bond
options.explanation: There is no initial double bond to add across.

options.text: Formation of a new carbon-carbon double bond
options.explanation: Elimination desaturates the chain by creating C=C.

questions.stem: In C2H4 + H2 -> C2H6, the double bond

options.text: Is consumed as the molecule becomes saturated
options.explanation: Addition saturates the alkene into an alkane.
Hydrogen addition destroys the double bond.
The product ethane has no double bond.
Nothing in the equation supports that.

questions.stem: Define an addition reaction.
questions.modelAnswer: A reaction in which two reactants combine to form a single product, typically across a carbon-carbon double bond.

questions.stem: State what elimination reactions typically produce.
questions.modelAnswer: An alkene plus a small eliminated molecule such as water or a hydrogen halide.

questions.stem: Explain why alkenes are the classic substrates for addition reactions.
questions.modelAnswer: The electron-rich double bond opens to accept two new substituents, converting the unsaturated alkene into a saturated single product.

questions.stem: Classify: C2H4 + H2O -> C2H5OH and CH3CH2Br -> C2H4 + HBr. State the bond change in each.
questions.modelAnswer: First is addition: the C=C is consumed. Second is elimination: a new C=C is created as HBr is ejected.

questions.stem: In CH3CH2Br + OH- -> C2H5OH + Br-, the hydroxide has

options.explanation: Hydroxide is consumed into the product.

options.text: Replaced the bromine atom on the carbon chain
options.explanation: The bromo group is swapped for hydroxyl - the substitution signature.
No oxygen gas forms; hydroxide becomes part of the alcohol.
Bromoethane has no double bond.

questions.stem: Organic oxidation can be described as

options.text: Replacement of one group by another
options.explanation: That is substitution.
That is hydrolysis.

options.text: Loss of hydrogen or gain of oxygen by the organic molecule
options.explanation: Both descriptions track the oxidation ladder's climb.

options.text: Gain of hydrogen or loss of oxygen
options.explanation: Those describe reduction.

questions.stem: CH3CHO + [O] -> CH3COOH shows

options.text: An acid reduced to an aldehyde
options.explanation: The arrow runs from aldehyde to acid, uphill the oxidation ladder.

options.text: A substitution of hydrogen by oxygen
options.explanation: The transformation is oxidation, not a positional swap.
No water is eliminated here.

options.text: An aldehyde oxidised to a carboxylic acid
options.explanation: Ethanal gains oxygen, climbing to ethanoic acid.

questions.stem: Which reagent could supply the [O] in the aldehyde oxidation?

options.text: Acidified potassium dichromate(VI), Fehling's solution or Tollens' reagent
options.explanation: All three are standard aldehyde oxidising agents.
That is a reducing agent, supplying [H].
No oxidising power there.
Solvents do not oxidise.

questions.stem: The oxidising agent in CH3CHO + [O] -> CH3COOH is itself

options.explanation: No such product is implied.

options.text: Reduced, as it accepts electrons from the aldehyde
options.explanation: Oxidation and reduction always pair; the agent comes down.

options.text: Oxidised, donating electrons to the aldehyde
options.explanation: The agent receives electrons; it is reduced.
The agent is consumed in stoichiometric redox.

questions.stem: Define a substitution reaction.
questions.modelAnswer: A reaction swapping an atom or group inside a compound for a different atom or group.

questions.stem: Name two oxidising agents used for aldehyde oxidation.
questions.modelAnswer: Acidified potassium dichromate(VI) and Tollens' reagent (or Fehling's solution).

questions.stem: Explain why the conversion of an aldehyde to a carboxylic acid is oxidation.
questions.modelAnswer: The molecule gains oxygen (equivalently loses relative hydrogen content), raising its position on the oxidation ladder while the reagent is reduced.

questions.stem: Classify CH3CH2Br + OH- -> C2H4 + H2O + Br- versus the same reagents giving C2H5OH + Br-. What single condition change steers between them?
questions.modelAnswer: First is elimination, second substitution; switching from ethanolic to aqueous hydroxide conditions steers the reaction from elimination toward substitution.

questions.stem: CH3CHO + [H] -> CH3CH2OH is

options.explanation: No water acts in this equation.
No atom is swapped in place; the whole molecule is reduced.

options.text: Reduction, gaining hydrogen to form the alcohol
options.explanation: Hydrogen gain marks reduction, descending from aldehyde to alcohol.
Hydrogen is gained here, not lost.

questions.stem: Which reagent typically supplies the [H] for aldehyde reduction?

options.explanation: That oxidises; it cannot supply hydrogen.
Another oxidising agent for aldehydes.
Not a hydride donor in this context.
LiAlH4 is the standard hydride donor for carbonyl reduction.

questions.stem: Hydrolysis of CH3Cl gives

options.explanation: Water splits the C-Cl bond, installing OH on carbon and taking Cl as HCl.
No such split occurs.
Neither product appears in hydrolysis.
That is the starting material unchanged.

questions.stem: The word hydrolysis literally suggests

options.explanation: No combustion is implied.
Hydro (water) plus lysis (splitting) names the mechanism.
That is hydrogenation, not hydrolysis.
That is reduction's oxygen side.

questions.stem: Organic reduction differs from organic oxidation because reduction

options.explanation: Oxygen gain is oxidation.
Reduction applies across many functional groups.

options.text: Gains hydrogen or loses oxygen, descending the oxidation ladder
options.explanation: Reduction runs the ladder's downhill direction.
Water is the hydrolysis reagent, not reduction's.

questions.stem: Define a hydrolysis reaction.
questions.modelAnswer: A reaction in which water splits a compound, its fragments installing across the broken bond.

questions.stem: State the organic products of reducing ethanal with [H].
Explain why aldehyde-to-alcohol conversion is reduction.
questions.modelAnswer: The molecule gains hydrogen (equivalently loses relative oxygen content), moving down the oxidation ladder while the hydride donor is oxidised.

questions.stem: A student mixes chloromethane with water and detects an acidic product. Identify the products and classify the reaction.
questions.modelAnswer: Methanol and hydrogen chloride form; the HCl explains the acidity, and the reaction is hydrolysis - water splitting the halogenoalkane.

questions.stem: Addition polymerisation works by

options.text: Splitting a polymer with water into monomers
options.explanation: That is the reverse idea, hydrolysis of polymers.
No substitution occurs; monomers simply link.
No combustion is involved.

options.text: Breaking open alkene double bonds to link monomers into a chain
options.explanation: The spent double bonds become the single-bond backbone of the polymer.

questions.stem: In the polymer from 1,2-dichloroethene, the repeat unit

options.text: Carries the two chlorine atoms on its two carbons, with the double bond consumed
options.explanation: The monomer's substituents ride into the repeat unit intact.

options.text: Loses its chlorine atoms during polymerisation
options.explanation: Addition polymerisation conserves all atoms.

options.text: Keeps its double bond inside the chain
options.explanation: The double bond is spent making the links.

options.text: Gains extra carbons from the catalyst
options.explanation: No carbons are added; the catalyst is not part of the chain.

questions.stem: The polymer backbone of an addition polymer consists of

options.explanation: The chain is covalent throughout.

options.text: Single carbon-carbon bonds linking the repeat units
options.explanation: Spent double bonds become the saturated backbone.
The double bonds are consumed in linking.
Halogen bonds are side substituents, not backbone.

questions.stem: Which statement about atom conservation in addition polymerisation is correct?

options.text: Half the monomer mass becomes waste
options.explanation: Nothing is wasted in addition polymerisation.

options.text: Only carbon and hydrogen enter the chain
options.explanation: Substituents like chlorine enter too.

options.text: Every atom of every monomer appears in the polymer
options.explanation: Addition polymerisation loses nothing - n monomers give one chain of n repeat units.

options.text: Small molecules are eliminated as the chain grows
options.explanation: That describes condensation polymerisation, not addition.

questions.stem: The monomer for a poly(alkene) must contain

options.explanation: Alkynes are not the AS-level polymerisation case.
Halogen-free alkenes like ethene polymerise readily.
Esters belong to condensation chemistry.
The openable double bond is the polymerisation handle.

questions.stem: State what happens to the alkene double bond during addition polymerisation.
questions.modelAnswer: It breaks open, and its electrons form the single bonds joining monomers into the chain.

questions.stem: Name the polymerisation type known at AS level.
Explain why addition polymerisation conserves atoms completely.
questions.modelAnswer: No small molecule is eliminated: the chain is simply the monomers' atoms relinked through spent double bonds, so n monomers give a repeat-unit chain carrying every atom.

questions.stem: A polymer sample is poly(1,2-dichloroethene). State the monomer and the fate of its double bond.
questions.modelAnswer: The monomer is 1,2-dichloroethene; its double bond breaks open and becomes the single-bond linkage within the chain, both chlorine atoms riding on the repeat unit.
